title: The Reckoning at Home
notebook: Vyktor: a Tyvaren intelligence officer defected to Orythia and described an active mole in my government.
The mole is a mid-ranking official with routine document access. The debrief is in Vyktor's office.
Liora gave Nadia grandfather's papers. Tomas says school isn't working. Jonas asks if his wife is still here.
location: Chancellor's Residence — Living Room, Evening, Week Thirty-Eight

narrative.text: Before you leave the office for the family meeting, Vyktor intercepts you in the corridor. His expression is unusual — not his normal analytical reserve, but something closer to urgency. 'Chancellor. A Tyvaren intelligence officer has defected to Orythia. Dorne received the debriefing notes an hour ago. The defector described an active mole in the Veltrian government — a mid-ranking official with routine access to military and diplomatic documents. The description narrows the field. Significantly. I have the debrief in my office. It can wait until tomorrow. Or it cannot. Your call.'

The living room of the Chancellor's residence has never felt like your living room. The furniture belongs to the state. The paintings on the walls were selected by a committee in the Halvek era and never replaced — landscapes of Veltrian countryside that look nothing like the actual countryside, idealized versions of a nation that did not exist when they were painted and does not exist now. But tonight the room is full of your family, all three of them, and the furniture might as well be yours for the weight of what is about to be said in it.

Jonas called this meeting. He did not call it a meeting — he said 'we need to talk, all of us, before things get worse' — but you recognize the structure. He has prepared. The architect's mind: understand the load-bearing elements before you propose changes. He is sitting in the chair by the cold fireplace, the same chair where he waited in the dark with his list of seventeen cancellations. That was fifteen weeks ago. The list has grown. Neither of you has mentioned it.

I asked everyone to be here because I think we need to say things that have been — stored. Not postponed, exactly. Stored. The way you store things you intend to deal with later, and then later becomes much later, and then you stop thinking of them as stored and start thinking of them as the way things are. I don't want the way things are to be the way things stay without anyone having chosen it.

Liora is twenty-two now. She is sitting on the arm of the sofa, not in it — the posture of someone who may need to leave quickly. She has the same sharpness around the eyes that you recognize from photographs of yourself at her age, the particular intensity of a young woman who has decided that politeness is a form of dishonesty and has stopped practicing it. Tomas is fourteen. He is in the corner of the sofa with his knees pulled up, which makes him look younger than fourteen and also older, the particular paradox of adolescents who have been through things they don't know how to name. He is looking at the floor. He has been looking at the floor a lot lately.

I'll start, since someone has to. I've been working with Nadia Voss for the past three months. Research, not writing. She published her investigation last week — you know that, obviously. What you may not know is that I gave her access to some of grandfather's papers. The ones you said were too sensitive to release. I made a copy before you had them sealed. I'm not apologizing for it. I'm telling you because you're going to find out anyway, and I'd rather you hear it from me than from a newspaper correction. I think the public has a right to know what happened in 1947, and I think you were wrong to keep it from them. I also think you were scared, and I understand why. Both things are true.

She is not attacking you. She is informing you. There is a difference, and the fact that she understands the difference at twenty-two is either a testament to her maturity or an indictment of the childhood that forced her to develop it. She released your father's papers to a journalist who then published them during a national crisis. She did it deliberately, with full knowledge of the consequences. And she is telling you directly, in person, because she believes that directness is what you owe each other. Some part of you — the part that is her mother rather than the Chancellor — is proud of her for having the courage to do both things. The other part is calculating the political damage and coming up with a number you don't want to look at.

I don't have anything prepared. I just — I need to say that school isn't working. I've tried. I've really tried. But every time I walk in there, people know who I am, and half of them hate me because of what you're doing and the other half expect me to be something I'm not. I can't be the Chancellor's son and also be a person. I don't know how to do both. And the Ironborn — I know you don't want me near them. I know. But they don't look at me like I'm supposed to be something. They just — they let me be there. I'm not saying I believe what they believe. I'm saying I don't know what I believe and they're the only ones who don't make me feel stupid for not knowing.

The room is quiet in the way rooms are quiet after someone says something true that has been true for a long time without being said. Jonas is watching you. Liora is watching you. Tomas is still looking at the floor, but his shoulders are set in the particular way of someone who has said the hard thing and is now waiting to find out whether saying it was a mistake. Outside, the city is dark. The Tyvaren deadline is somewhere between expired and about to expire. The military is either mobilized against a foreign enemy or mobilized against you, depending on last week's decisions. The economy is in whatever state thirty-eight weeks of crisis have left it. All of these things are happening. And also your family is here, in this room, asking you to look at what thirty-eight weeks have cost them.

I'm going to say something and I need you to hear all of it before you respond. I love you. I have loved you since we were twenty-three years old and you told me you were going to change the country and I believed you because you believed you. I still believe you. But I cannot be married to the Chancellorship. I can be married to you — the person, the woman I married, the woman who still exists somewhere under the briefings and the crisis meetings and the decisions that never stop. But if that woman isn't coming back — if the Chancellorship is all there is now — I need to know. Because I have been waiting, and I will keep waiting if there's something to wait for, but I won't keep waiting if there isn't. That's not an ultimatum. That's me telling you where I am, because I haven't been telling you, and the not-telling has become its own thing between us.

Three people. Three different kinds of need. Liora needs you to respect her choices even when those choices hurt you politically. Tomas needs you to see him as a person rather than as a political vulnerability. Jonas needs you to tell him whether the woman he married still exists. None of these needs can be met with a policy response. None of them respond to the skills you have spent thirty-eight weeks developing. The Chancellor cannot answer what your family is asking. Only Katerin can answer it. And Katerin has been subordinated to the Chancellor for so long that you are not entirely sure she still knows how to speak.

choices.text: "Jonas — the woman you married is here. She's exhausted and she's made mistakes and she has been so focused on not losing the country that she didn't notice she was losing you. All three of you. Liora, I'm not angry about the papers. I'm hurt you didn't tell me first, but I understand why you didn't, and I'm — I'm proud that you had the conviction to make your own choice even knowing I'd disagree. Tomas, the Ironborn are not the answer, but I hear you that school is breaking something in you and I should have seen it sooner. We're going to figure out something different. Not next week. Now. The country will survive one evening without me. It might not survive me losing you."
choices.tooltip: Choose your family, fully and publicly. The most human option. May cost you politically — but some things matter more than politics.

choices.text: "I can't give you everything you're asking for — not honestly, not with what's coming. But I can give you the truth. Liora: what you did was a betrayal of my trust, and I need time to process that, but I respect that you made a principled choice and I'm not going to punish you for being the kind of person who makes principled choices. Tomas: the Ironborn are dangerous, not because of what they say to you but because of what they will ask you to do eventually, and I'm going to help you find something else that gives you the same sense of belonging without the cost. Jonas — I don't know if the woman you married is still here. I think she is. I think she's buried under things that feel essential but may not be. I'm asking you to help me dig her out. I'm not asking you to wait indefinitely. I'm asking you to try, with me, for a defined period, and then we reassess honestly. That's not the answer you wanted. It's the most honest one I have."
choices.tooltip: Honest about your limitations. Doesn't fix everything but opens a path to repair. Requires follow-through.

choices.text: "I hear all of you. I do. And I am asking you to hear me: there are forty thousand Tyvaren soldiers on our border. The military may or may not be loyal — I will know more in the morning. The economy is balanced on decisions I have to make in the next seventy-two hours. I cannot — I physically cannot — do this conversation justice right now. I am not saying no. I am saying not tonight. I need you to give me until this crisis passes, and then we will have this conversation properly, with the time and attention it deserves. I know you've heard that before. I know. But this time I am naming it — I am telling you explicitly that this is deferred, not denied. Can you give me that?"
choices.tooltip: Defer the reckoning again. Each deferral costs more than the last. The crisis may never 'pass' — and they know it.

choices.text: "You want me to apologize for governing? For doing the job I was elected to do? Liora, you leaked classified family documents to a journalist during a national security crisis — that is not 'making a principled choice,' that is undermining your own mother while foreign tanks are on the border. Tomas, you've been skipping school to spend time with a nationalist youth organization that wants to overthrow the government I lead — do you understand what that looks like? What it does to my ability to govern when my own son is being photographed with people who want me removed? Jonas — I understand you're hurting. But I am trying to hold this country together, and I cannot do that while also managing three separate emotional crises at home. I need you to be stronger than this. All of you. We can revisit when the immediate threat has passed."
choices.tooltip: Turn the accusation back on them. May feel justified in the moment — but the damage to your family may be permanent.

choices.text: "Tomas — I'm going to talk to you first, because you're the one I've been most afraid to talk to. I know what it feels like to be the child of someone everyone has an opinion about. My father was executed when I was young. For years afterward, people looked at me the way they look at you now — like I was either a victim or a threat, never just a person. I survived it because someone — my mother — kept treating me like a person even when I was making choices that scared her. I'm not going to tell you to stay away from the Ironborn. I'm going to ask you to talk to me about what you find there, honestly, so I can understand it instead of just fearing it. And I'm going to ask you to keep talking to me even when it's hard, because the alternative — the silence — that's what actually breaks families. Not the disagreements. The silence after them."
choices.tooltip: Reach Tomas through shared experience — the burden of being a political child. The most targeted intervention for the most vulnerable family member.

choices.text: "The defector debrief cannot wait. Tell Jonas I will be thirty minutes late. If there is a Tyvaren spy in my government giving my family something to mourn at a funeral instead of a kitchen table, I need to know before I sit down with them."
